tx.t: This lecture is about the short history of the internet. The first network, ARPANET, linked four American research sites in nineteen sixty-nine.

In nineteen seventy-one, Ray Tomlinson sent the first email between computers and chose the at sign for addresses. Tim Berners-Lee, a British scientist working at CERN, invented the World Wide Web at the end of the nineteen eighties.

The web and the internet are not the same thing: the internet is the network, and the web is one service that runs on it. Google was founded in nineteen ninety-eight by two students at Stanford University.
Today, more than five billion people use the internet.

tx.t: In today's lecture, I will talk about the growth of cities. In two thousand and seven, for the first time in history, more than half of the world's people lived in cities.
The United Nations expects the figure to reach about two thirds by twenty fifty. Cities take up only about two per cent of the Earth's land, but they produce most of the world's wealth.
Rapid growth can cause housing shortages, traffic jams and air pollution. Some cities are planting trees and building cycle lanes to make urban life healthier.

tx.t: Let us begin with the early history of the bicycle. The first machine of this kind was built in eighteen seventeen by a German baron called Karl von Drais, and it had no pedals.

In the eighteen sixties, pedals were fixed to the front wheel, and the machines were nicknamed boneshakers because of their hard wheels. In the eighteen seventies, the penny-farthing had a huge front wheel, which made it fast but dangerous.

The safety bicycle of the eighteen eighties had two wheels of the same size and a chain driving the back wheel. In eighteen eighty-eight, John Dunlop introduced the air-filled tyre, which made riding far more comfortable.

tx.t: In this lecture I will talk about the Great Wall of China. The wall was not built at one time. Different rulers built and rebuilt sections over more than two thousand years.

The first emperor of China, Qin Shi Huang, joined earlier walls together around two hundred and twenty-one BC. Most of the wall that tourists visit today was built in the Ming dynasty, from stone and brick.

A survey in two thousand and twelve measured all its sections at more than twenty-one thousand kilometres. It is a popular story that the wall can be seen from space with the naked eye, but this is not true.

It takes about twenty-seven days to orbit the Earth once. The same side of the Moon always faces us, because its rotation takes exactly as long as its orbit.
The Moon is about a quarter of the width of the Earth. Gravity on the Moon is only about one-sixth of gravity on Earth.
